source.title: Combatting Dimensional Collapse in LLM Pre-Training Data via Diversified File Selection
source.authors: Ziqing Fan; Si-Yuan Du; Sheng-Chao Hu; Pingjie Wang; Li Shen; Ya Zhang; Da-Cheng Tao; Yan-Feng Wang

record.file_problem: Whole paper and appendix are present. No material truncation or garbling affects the reported experiments.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies model size and evaluates downstream benchmark performance, which bears on V6. It does not use held-out cross-entropy loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream benchmark scores for models of different sizes, so those results bear on V6. It reports no held-out pretraining loss, power-law fits, large-run loss extrapolations, or compute-optimal parameter/token split. The mention of Hoffmann et al. is background, not a test of those results. Table 2 also reports individual task scores; the rows below record its separately reported average metric across seven tasks.
record.test_reason: This is a data-selection paper. As a by-product, it reports seven-task Harness average accuracy for TinyLlama 120M, 560M and 1.1B, each trained from scratch at fixed token budgets (10B, 50B) under eight selection methods. The size trend bears weakly on V6 in a data-subset setting. There are only three sizes, with no fit, no uncertainty on the averages, and no loss-to-task mapping. It is not a test of V1–V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that diversified file selection (DiSF) mitigates dimensional collapse and improves average downstream performance and training/data efficiency. They draw no conclusions about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study selects pretraining files by embedding-space diversity and evaluates downstream task scores across model sizes; it does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported downstream averages vary with file-selection method and training budget. The size trend is reported separately for these conditions.
record.problems: Only three TinyLlama sizes are compared for the relevant downstream trend; the paper reports no predictive fit or uncertainty for the Table 2 average scores. These experiments do not establish power-law scaling or generalize beyond the tested settings.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports individual scores for seven tasks, in addition to the average recorded here; those task-level results are omitted rather than selectively sampling them. Table 3 reports MMLU and BBH results at TinyLlama 1.1B, and Tables 4, 7, and 8 report additional architecture/data settings, but they do not add a comparable three-size downstream sweep.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss reported or fitted.
No power-law test in other modalities or regimes.
Predictability is not tested: there is no fitted relationship, no prediction of larger models, and no link from pretraining loss to task score. Only monotonic increase over three sizes is shown.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Average performance versus pre-trained tokens (curves) for DiSF and Full Data at three sizes. Bears on V6 scaling with data.
Size trend 120M→560M→1.1B under three feature extractors (CLIP 39.5/42.1/43.9; Contriever 40.6/43.1/45.2; GPT-2 40.0/42.3/44.4)
Task-level non-monotonicity with size: at 50B, Random BoolQ goes 59.0→56.2 from 560M to 1.1B, and WinoGrande is flat. The average hides these.

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence for V6. The size comparison is incidental to a method benchmark: three sizes, one architecture family, no fit and no error bars on the averages. Several tasks (ARC-c, OBQA, WinoGrande) sit near chance.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy sweep or power-law loss fit.
No fit on small runs or prediction of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute search for loss-minimizing parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law loss across modalities or the listed training regimes.
The paper reports average downstream scores at three TinyLlama sizes, but does not fit a predictive relationship, test prediction from pretraining loss, or establish a general scaling law.
No comparison of fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Seven-task Harness average, TinyLlama 120M→560M→1.1B, all eight selection methods, 10B and 50B token budgets
relationships.reason: The average rises at each size step for every method and budget, e.g. Random at 50B: 38.9→41.6→42.9 (t2-50-*-560/1p1, t2-10-*-560/1p1). The evidence is monotonic, not shown predictable.
relationships.display_finding: Average performance rises at each size step for all eight methods at both token budgets, including random selection at 50B tokens from 38.9 to 41.6 to 42.9.

relationships.reason: Gains shrink to about 0.5 points for Random and QuRating-A (t2-10-rand-1p1, t2-10-qa-1p1), with no reported uncertainty. At small token budgets, extra parameters barely move the average.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing parameters from 560M to 1.1B added about 0.5 points for Random and QuRating-A, without reported uncertainty.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Average seven-task Harness performance for the eight reported selection methods, TinyLlama 120M to 1.1B, at 10B or 50B training tokens
reader_labels.reason: For every method and budget, the reported average rises at each successive tested size; rows t2-10-rand-560 through t2-10-disf-1p1 and t2-50-rand-560 through t2-50-disf-1p1 record those increases. This is evidence of a monotonic trend in this setting, not a fitted predictive law.
